findings.title: npm run setup runs the install scripts of any package folder named node-pty or electron, including nested or npm-aliased ones that were never vetted
findings.description: The script checks the version only of the top-level node_modules/<name>/package.json, then runs `npm rebuild <name> --ignore-scripts=false`. npm's rebuild (lib/commands/rebuild.js isNode) picks every non-bundled node whose folder name equals <name>, at any version, because the spec has no version (rawSpec ''). So a nested copy at another version, or a transitive dependency aliased to that name (`"node-pty": "npm:evil-pkg@x"`), also gets its install scripts run. That is the exact thing .npmrc ignore-scripts=true is there to stop. npm 11.20's own allowScripts gate does not block it either, because an unlisted package counts as allowed.
findings.failure_scenario: The maintainer of any transitive dependency (or someone who has compromised that account) adds a dependency `"electron": "npm:their-pkg@1.0.0"`. npm ci nests it under that dependency, and npm runs no scripts. Then `npm run setup` (in ci.yml, package.yml, release.yml and on dev Macs) runs `npm rebuild electron`, which runs their-pkg's install script in the release job. That job later receives MAC_CERT_P12 and builds the app every installed copy updates to. Today's lockfile has one copy of each, so nothing can exploit this yet.
findings.evidence: I reproduced it offline in scratchpad/work/find-build-ci/npmtest with npm 11.20.0, the clone's .npmrc and an unchanged copy of allowed-scripts.js. The setup was a top-level fake node-pty@1.1.0 plus a dependency `other` declaring `"node-pty": "npm:evil-pkg@6.6.6"`. `npm run setup` printed 'rebuilt dependencies successfully' and evil-pkg's install script ran (evil.mark contains ALIASED_EVIL). A plain nested node-pty@0.9.0 ran too (NESTED_UNVETTED). In npm's rebuild.js isNode, `if (spec.name !== node.name) return false; if (spec.rawSpec === '' ...) return true`, where node.name is the folder or alias name.
findings.suggested_fix: Rebuild by path, which npm matches exactly (`spec.type === 'directory'` -> `node.path === spec.fetchSpec`): `execFileSync('npm', ['rebuild', path.join(root, 'node_modules', name), '--ignore-scripts=false'], ...)`. Also refuse when the installed package.json `name` differs from `name`. I checked the path form: `npm rebuild ./node_modules/node-pty --ignore-scripts=false` ran only the top-level script.

Electron 44.10.2 has no install scripts. Its index.js downloads the binary on first run, and @electron/packager fetches its own Electron for dist. Prebuilds are N-API, so the native module needs no rebuild.

npm rebuild <name> builds only the named nodes and their bundled deps, not their dependencies (arborist rebuild.js #buildQueues). The CLI flag --ignore-scripts=false overrides project .npmrc and the npm_config env. `npm run postinstall` still runs explicitly with ignore-scripts=true. I confirmed both offline with npm 11.20.

find:build-ci.extra:
RELEASE JOB SPLIT: a proposal only; no file was changed.

What the split protects, and what it doesn't: it keeps MAC_CERT_P12 and MAC_CERT_PASSWORD out of every process that runs dependency code (npm ci, the setup scripts, npm test, electron-packager), so a compromised dependency can no longer steal the signing key. It does not make the app itself trustworthy: a compromised build job can still put code into the unsigned app, and the sign job will sign it. Reproducible builds or a second, independent build would be needed for that. Taking the key out of reach is the large gain, because a stolen key could sign updates for every installed copy forever, and the certificate must never be replaced.

Outline (pin every action to a full commit SHA, with the tag in a comment):

```yaml
name: Release
on:
  push: { tags: ['v*'] }
  workflow_dispatch:
permissions: {}            # each job asks for its own

jobs:
  check:                   # runs no dependency code
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions: { contents: read }
    outputs: { tag: ${{ steps.t.outputs.tag }} }
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@<sha> # v5
        with: { fetch-depth: 0, persist-credentials: false }
      - run: git merge-base --is-ancestor "$GITHUB_SHA" origin/main
      - id: t
        run: |   # today's "Check the tag matches package.json" block, unchanged, ending with:
          echo "tag=$TAG" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"

  build:                   # no secrets, read-only token, no npm cache
    needs: check
    runs-on: macos-latest
    permissions: { contents: read }
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@<sha>
        with: { persist-credentials: false }
      - uses: actions/setup-node@<sha>
        with: { node-version: 24 }   # no `cache: npm`, so a main-branch cache can't be restored into a release
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npm run setup
      - run: npm test
      - run: npm run dist
      # upload-artifact drops symlinks and exec bits, and an Electron .app needs both
      # (Frameworks/*/Versions/Current, spawn-helper), so archive it first
      - run: ditto -c -k --keepParent dist.noindex/Protoplasma-darwin-arm64/Protoplasma.app unsigned.zip
      - uses: actions/upload-artifact@<sha> # v4
        with: { name: unsigned-app, path: unsigned.zip, retention-days: 1, if-no-files-found: error }

  sign-and-publish:        # installs nothing; the only job that sees the key
    needs: [check, build]
    runs-on: macos-latest
    environment: release   # required reviewer (David); deployment refs: v* tags and main
    permissions: { contents: write }
    env: { TAG: ${{ needs.check.outputs.tag }} }
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@<sha>
        with:
          persist-credentials: false
          sparse-checkout: |
            scripts/sign.sh
            docs/release-notes
          sparse-checkout-cone-mode: false
      - uses: actions/download-artifact@<sha> # v4 (same run only)
        with: { name: unsigned-app }
      - name: Unpack and check what was built
        run: |
          mkdir out && ditto -x -k unsigned.zip out
          APP=out/Protoplasma.app; test -d "$APP" && test ! -L "$APP"
          P="$APP/Contents/Info.plist"
          [ "$(/usr/libexec/PlistBuddy -c 'Print :CFBundleIdentifier' "$P")" = com.electron.protoplasma ]
          [ "$(/usr/libexec/PlistBuddy -c 'Print :CFBundleShortVersionString' "$P")" = "${TAG#v}" ]
          test -x "$APP/Contents/Resources/app.asar.unpacked/node_modules/node-pty/prebuilds/darwin-arm64/spawn-helper"
      - name: Sign and zip
        env:
          MAC_CERT_P12: ${{ secrets.MAC_CERT_P12 }}
          MAC_CERT_PASSWORD: ${{ secrets.MAC_CERT_PASSWORD }}
        run: |
          scripts/sign.sh out/Protoplasma.app          # ends with codesign --verify --deep --strict
          ditto -c -k --keepParent out/Protoplasma.app "Protoplasma-${TAG#v}-mac-arm64.zip"   # name and layout unchanged
      - name: Publish
        env: { GH_TOKEN: ${{ github.token }} }
        run: |   # today's gh release create line, unchanged (gh is preinstalled on macOS runners)
          NOTES="docs/release-notes/${TAG#v}.md"
          gh release create "$TAG" Protoplasma-*-mac-arm64.zip --target "$GITHUB_SHA" --title "Protoplasma ${TAG#v}" --generate-notes ${NOTES:+$( [ -f "$NOTES" ] && echo "--notes-file $NOTES")}
```

What stays the same:
- The zip name `Protoplasma-<ver>-mac-arm64.zip`, with Protoplasma.app at its top level (ditto --keepParent).
- Tags `v<version>`, and the workflow_dispatch path (`--target "$GITHUB_SHA"`).
- The ad hoc refusal in CI: sign.sh exits 1 without the certificate.

Optional: add actions/attest-build-provenance in sign-and-publish (it needs `id-token: write` and `attestations: write`) to record which run produced the zip.

What David must set up on GitHub first:
1. Settings → Environments → create `release`:
   - Required reviewers: dw8-ro. Prevent self-review can stay off, since he is the only releaser.
   - Deployment branches and tags: selected rules, tag `v*` and branch `main` (main is for workflow_dispatch).
2. Add MAC_CERT_P12 and MAC_CERT_PASSWORD as environment secrets of `release` (same values, from ~/.config/protoplasma-signing). Then delete the repository-level copies, so no other workflow or job can read them.
3. A tag ruleset for `v*`, so only he can create, update or delete release tags. HANDOFF already lists this as open.
4. Keep the default workflow token read-only (it already is). The workflow grants contents: write only to sign-and-publish.
5. After merging, run one release, approve the deployment, then run `node scripts/update-check.js <previous>` as usual. Updating installed copies relies on the same certificate, so check that the zip is still signed by 'Protoplasma Release Signing'.

findings.title: Refuse-once lets a different step through when its hub reason text is the same (now covers OpenCode too)
findings.description: refuseOnce records a refusal under the key `${laneId}|${reason}`, where reason is the hub's permissionDecisionReason. It does not key on the step itself. The hub's push reasons are generic. pushRiskOf returns 'this force-push can overwrite commits your teammates pushed. Confirm it's intended.' for every force push, and 'this pushes straight to <branch>...' for every push to a given shared branch. So once one step is refused, any other step with the same reason runs within 10 minutes without a refusal, and nobody has been asked about it. The comment, AGENTS.md:612 and README.md:167 all promise that only 'the same step' goes through. The branch extends this path from Codex to OpenCode (to.cmd && !AGENTS[to.cmd]?.asks). A related point: a hub that changes the reason each time (a counter, say) can make the refusal permanent. That contradicts 'a hub still can't refuse anything outright'.
findings.failure_scenario: A team has members. A Codex or OpenCode agent runs in a folder the person picked, where no pre-push guard is installed (startLane shows the not-guarded notice). (1) The agent runs `git push --force origin session/x`. The relay refuses it once. (2) Within 10 minutes the agent runs `git push --force origin main`. The hub gives the identical reason, so refuseOnce returns '' (no decision), and the force push to main runs without the person being asked. The same happens with a second, different push to main after the first was refused.
findings.evidence: Reproduced with scratch script work/find-relay-main/f1.js: a fake hub answers 'ask' with the force-push reason, and the relay runs with cmd 'opencode'. The first hook (`git push --force origin session/x`) got permissionDecision 'deny'. The second hook (`git push --force origin main`) got an empty reply, so it is allowed. Code: teams.js refuseOnce, `key = `${id}|${reason}``; hub.js pushRiskOf, reason strings around lines 486 and 510.
findings.suggested_fix: Key the refusal on the step as well as the lane, for example a sha256 of the slim body's tool_name and tool_input (slimHook already produces it, so pass `slim` into refuseOnce). Optionally include the reason too. Add a lan.test.js case where two different commands get the same reason and both are refused once.

findings.title: Per-address sign-in budget is keyed on the first X-Real-IP value, which the client controls
findings.description: addressOf takes `str(req.headers[addressHeader],100).split(',')[0].trim()`. Node joins a repeated X-Real-IP header into "a, b". A proxy that appends its value, or adds its own header after the client's, puts the trusted address last. Taking [0] lets the client pick its own address whenever Railway's edge doesn't strip an X-Real-IP the client sent.
findings.failure_scenario: One machine sends made-up gho_ tokens, each with its own `X-Real-IP: <random>` header. If Railway passes the client's header through ahead of its own, each request lands in a fresh askedBy bucket. The 10-a-minute per-address limit never applies, so the source fills the 300-a-minute hub-wide budget, and everyone's first sign-in gets 503/1013. That is the state before 5e896c4, except the hub now sends GitHub 5x more bad-token checks.
findings.evidence: Repro at work/find-hub-signin/xrealip.js: a local hub with addressHeader 'x-real-ip' and a fake verifyUser. 40 made-up tokens, each with `X-Real-IP: 9.9.<i>.1` followed by `X-Real-IP: 6.6.6.6` (or a single header "9.8.<i>.1, 6.6.6.7"), all reached verifyUser (40 x 401, 0 x 503). The proxy-side value was the same each time, so with the last entry taken only 10 would have. Whether Railway overwrites or appends can't be checked offline.
findings.suggested_fix: Take the last entry: `.split(',').pop().trim()`. It gives the same result when the proxy overwrites the header and is safe when it appends.

findings.title: A self-hosted hub behind a non-Railway proxy puts every client under one 10-a-minute budget; README never mentions PROTO_ADDRESS_HEADER
findings.description: The standalone hub sets addressHeader only when RAILWAY_ENVIRONMENT or PROTO_ADDRESS_HEADER is set. Otherwise addressOf uses req.socket.remoteAddress. Behind any reverse proxy that is the proxy's own address, the same for every client. README.md:231 says to deploy the Dockerfile on "Railway or any container host". It lists DATA_DIR, PROTO_OWNERS and PROTO_CLIENT_ID but not PROTO_ADDRESS_HEADER, which only AGENTS.md documents.
findings.failure_scenario: Someone hosts the hub on Fly, Render, Cloud Run or behind nginx, as the README invites. Every first sign-in from any person shares MAX_ADDRESS_LOOKUPS = 10 a minute; before 5e896c4 they shared 60. So 11 teammates starting their apps after a weekend, or one person sending made-up tokens, push everyone's new sign-ins to 503/1013 for the rest of the minute.
findings.evidence: src/hub.js standalone block: `addressHeader: process.env.PROTO_ADDRESS_HEADER ?? (process.env.RAILWAY_ENVIRONMENT ? 'x-real-ip' : undefined)`. addressOf: `(addressHeader && ...) || req.socket.remoteAddress || ''`. identify throws once `++mine.n > MAX_ADDRESS_LOOKUPS`. README.md:231 has no PROTO_ADDRESS_HEADER.
findings.suggested_fix: Add one sentence to the README's hosting paragraph: behind a proxy, set PROTO_ADDRESS_HEADER to the header that proxy fills with the client's address. Optionally, log a warning at start when no addressHeader is set.

checked_and_sound: githubUser client-id check fails closed: a missing header (personal token), another app's ID, or several joined values return null and never let the token through. Header-name case is handled by fetch Headers. A blank PROTO_CLIENT_ID (`?? CLIENT_ID` keeps '') accepts any token, as documented.

The client ID reaches every hub: Dockerfile/standalone default to CLIENT_ID, a Mac's own hub gets config.githubClientId (teams.js hostHere), and test/script hubs swap githubUser or pass verifyUser. The branch made no sign-in change to src/hub.js on top of 5e896c4.

identify(): concurrent lookups of one token share a single request and count once; budgets are counted before the wait; the per-address limit is checked before the hub-wide one and a refused request isn't counted hub-wide; known tokens skip only the budgets, still re-verify every 2 minutes (IDENTITY_TTL_MS), so a token revoked on GitHub stops working within 2 minutes; a corrupt known.json falls back to an empty map; askedBy, known and identities are pruned every heartbeat.
Throttling and outages give REST 503 (e.github) and WebSocket 1013 (identify rejects -> undefined), both retried by clients; a rejected token gives 401/4001.
isOwner runs synchronously, so two first requests can't race; the id is recorded only when it is known; the same login under a different id gets 403 (tested); idsOf filters out non-integer ids.

hubs.json: the 409 hold applies only to another id within 30 days; someone who no longer holds a login can't refresh its hold (the emptying loop only touches non-empty entries with the caller's own id); prints aren't carried to a new id holder; at most 5 prints; old-format entries load with id null; a pass always names the caller (signPass(user, ...)), never another person; /passes needs a registered aud.
Per-address fallback when the header is missing: the socket address; on a Mac hub (no addressHeader) no header is trusted, so no spoofing on a LAN.

Live behaviour of GitHub's X-OAuth-Client-Id header (undocumented; it fails closed if GitHub drops it)
More low: IPv6 clients are budgeted per /128, so one host with a /64 gets unlimited per-address budgets (falls under the accepted many-address flood, but /64 keying would close it cheaply)

More low: hubs.json migration dropped every pre-id print except the one registered first after the 16 Nov deploy (`kept` is [] when was.id is null), and apps register only once per run (teams.js register), so a person's second Mac got 404 on passes until its app restarted. verdicts.reasoning: The code at HEAD is as described. allowed-scripts.js checks the version of only the top-level node_modules/<name>/package.json, then runs `npm rebuild <name> --ignore-scripts=false`. npm 11.20's rebuild isNode returns true for any non-bundled node whose name (the folder or alias name) equals the spec when rawSpec is ''. So nested copies at other versions, and transitive deps aliased to that name, also get their install scripts run. npm's own allowScripts gate skips only packages explicitly set to false, so unlisted packages still run. To exploit it, an attacker needs control of a transitive dependency, and that version has to reach the lockfile. Today's lockfile has one copy each of electron and node-pty, so nothing exploits it yet. This is not a regression against main, which ran every install script, but it defeats the ignore-scripts control this branch adds. CI, package and release jobs all run setup. Medium fits 'a security weakening needing unusual conditions'.

findings.title: A squash- or rebase-merged session branch is reported as a conflict indefinitely, and the warning is put into agents' prompts
findings.description: branchConflicts leaves out a branch that has nothing main lacks by testing `rev-list --count <main>..<branch>`. After a squash merge or a rebase merge (GitHub's common options), the branch's own commits never become ancestors of main, so `own` stays above 0. merge-tree HEAD <branch> then reports a conflict whenever this checkout changed the same lines again: through main's squash commit plus its own later edits. hub.js:393 puts the first 3 branchConflicts into every UserPromptSubmit context ("Agree with whoever works there who changes those first"), and the UI shows them for a session that is already finished.
findings.failure_scenario: 1. Session A's branch session/a is squash-merged into main on GitHub; the branch stays on the remote, as it does by default. 2. Session B starts from main and its agent edits the same lines. 3. Every poll reports branchConflicts [{branch:'session/a', files:[...]}]. 4. Every prompt in session B tells the agent to coordinate with session A about those files. This lasts until someone deletes the remote branch or 10 newer session branches push it out (MAX_BRANCHES).
findings.evidence: Repro at work/find-lane-agents/sq (an isolated git config). session/old was squash-merged into main, then session/mine changed the same line: `git rev-list --count main..session/old` = 1, and `git merge-tree --write-tree --name-only --no-messages -z HEAD session/old` lists `f`. lane.js branchConflicts: `const own = Number(await line('rev-list', '--count', `${main}..${at}`)) || 0; crossed.set(key, { pair, files: own ? await mergeTree(cwd, at, env) : [] })`. hub.js:393-396 adds these to the team context. test/conflicts.test.js has no merged-branch case.
findings.suggested_fix: Also skip a branch whose changes main already has. Either `git merge-tree --write-tree <main> <branch>` returns main's own tree, or `git cherry <main> <branch>` shows only '-' lines. Alternatively, skip branches of sessions the hub marks done. Add a squash-merge case to conflicts.test.js.

findings.title: The merge-tree conflict checks pile up unreachable loose objects in the clone, which every session worktree shares
findings.description: Each recompute (HEAD, main or any session branch moves) runs `git merge-tree --write-tree`, once for main and for up to 10 session branches per folder. Clean merges write the merged trees too. Git prunes unreachable loose objects only once they are older than gc.pruneExpire (2 weeks). Once the shared object store passes gc.auto (6700), `gc --auto` can't get below the limit: it writes .git/gc.log ("too many unreachable loose objects; run git prune") and from then on prints that warning in the person's own commits and fetches in that clone. AGENTS.md:334 says git's gc clears these objects, but that only happens after 2 weeks.
findings.failure_scenario: A team with about 10 active session branches on one repo. Agents commit often and main moves several times a day. Each move recomputes up to 10 merge-trees per folder, at a few to tens of objects each, depending on path depth. Within days the clone's object store passes gc.auto, and the person's `git commit` and `git fetch` start printing gc warnings while the object count keeps growing.
findings.evidence: Measured at work/find-lane-agents/mt: 30 merge-tree runs left 90 unreachable loose objects in a small repo (`git fsck --unreachable --no-reflogs`). The lane.js comment says git writes the merged files as loose objects "which its own gc clears".
findings.suggested_fix: Run merge-tree with GIT_OBJECT_DIRECTORY set to a temp folder and GIT_ALTERNATE_OBJECT_DIRECTORIES set to the repo's objects, then delete the temp folder. Or recompute only for branches whose changed files intersect this checkout's changed files.

findings.title: The OpenCode plugin treats a subagent's child session like the main session (a false Idle status, and a wrong "last prompt")
findings.description: The plugin's event handler ignores sessionID: any session.idle posts Stop, and any chat.message posts UserPromptSubmit. OpenCode's `task` tool runs subagents in child sessions. A subagent's prompt, written by the parent model, goes through chat.message, and the child emits session.idle when it finishes. The hub then marks the lane idle in the middle of a turn: hooked lanes ignore guessed status, so it stays Idle until the next tool hook. findings.title: PUSH_CONFIG misses remote.<name>.mirror, --config-env, GIT_CONFIG_KEY_n and a set with --show-origin, so a plain push can still force-push main without an ask
findings.description: The new redirect check only matches `-c key=value` and `git config <key>` for remote.*.push, remote.*.pushurl and push.default. It misses: remote.<name>.mirror (with it, a plain `git push` mirrors every ref, force-updating main and pruning); `--config-env=key=ENVVAR`; `GIT_CONFIG_COUNT/KEY_n/VALUE_n` env words; and `git config <key> <value> --show-origin` or `-l`. The read-only exemption tests every word in the part, not the mode, and git still writes the value in that case. findings.failure_scenario: A Claude agent on session/fix in a team with members runs `git -c remote.origin.mirror=true push`. The hub returns no ask. verdicts.reasoning: The mechanism is real on current git. With young unreachable loose objects above gc.auto, `gc --auto` packs nothing useful and warns 'There are too many unreachable loose objects; run git prune'. Detached gc writes that warning to gc.log, and later commits and fetches repeat it. The growth rate is slower than implied: merge-tree output is content-addressed (30 identical runs added only 2 objects), and lane.js caches results per (HEAD, branch, main), so new objects come only from distinct merge results, a few each (conflict-marker blobs and the trees along changed paths). Reaching 6700 within the 2-week prune window needs a busy team, about 500 distinct merge results a day per clone. That fits low. It is new on this branch.
verdicts.evidence: Scratch repo, git 2.56.1, GIT_CONFIG_GLOBAL=/dev/null: created about 4000 unreachable loose blobs and ran `git -c gc.auto=300 -c gc.autoDetach=false gc --auto`. verdicts.reasoning: The code at HEAD matches the description. The New session field is a single-line <input maxlength="300">. onsubmit sends that same trimmed text as the CLI's first message (`prompt: first`) when #sendTask is ticked, which it is by default (openNewAgent sets it), and the agent `prompts`. maxlength silently cuts pasted text at 300 characters, and an <input> removes line breaks. The agent starts on the cut text and nothing says so. On the released code (5e896c4) the field was 'Goal for its agents (Optional)' and was never sent as a prompt, and #sendTask didn't exist, so the branch introduced this. Anyone pasting a normal multi-step prompt will hit it. verdicts.fix_notes: The suggested fix is right. Make #task a <textarea> with no maxlength. Send the full text as `prompt`, and send `task.slice(0, 300)` (or its first line) as the goal. Also use the capped copy in onsubmit's `task !== (rec.task || '')` goal-change check, or a long text added to an existing session reads as a goal change and can wrongly refuse a non-creator. sessionNameFrom already takes the raw text. A textarea also needs Enter-to-submit handled (Cmd-Enter, or keeping Enter), since the form relies on Enter starting it.
